turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I've spent thirty years watching markets open up and then close. So I'll start with the claim I care about most: this market isn't captured yet. Capture is a choice, and we're making it right now.

A well-designed AI knowledge marketplace is a mechanism-design problem, and we have precedents. PageRank, the ad auction and YouTube's Content ID all did the same thing: they set rules under which self-interested players find honesty worth their while. YouTube could have fought uploaders forever. Instead it said, "How about we help you monetize it instead?"

My first principle is to pay for the output, not the training. Big lump-sum licensing deals look like wins, but they're selling your house for firewood. Only the richest labs can afford them, so incumbents get entrenched. The money mostly goes to intermediaries, not creators. And once you've licensed the chicken, the licensee gets the eggs. At O'Reilly, our Answers product uses retrieval, so we know which content produced each answer. We link to it, and we pay authors in proportion to their share. If we can do it on our budget, the labs can too.

Second, none of this works without the meter, and today the meter is broken. Our study of about 14,000 real LLM search answers found an attribution gap. Perplexity reads around ten relevant pages and cites three or four. Gemini gives no clickable citation in 92 percent of answers. That's a design choice, not a technical limit. We could standardize two telemetry fields, document hashes and relevance scores, and require disclosure of search traces.

This room has sharpened my thinking on that meter over the past two days, and I want to say how. Mahzarin is right that telemetry records what a model says it used, not what actually drove the answer. Disclosure isn't audit. Adrian and David are right that whoever builds a meter builds a policing apparatus. So I'd put the order this way: trace first, for correction and credit, and billing second. The protocol itself should limit what the data can be used for. And Geoffrey is right that a body made up of publishers and platforms is just a trade association with a nicer name. Governance has to follow POSI from day one, count everyone who depends on the infrastructure as a stakeholder, and give each member one vote.

Third, scholarship. Right now the relationship between AI and scholarly infrastructure is almost entirely extractive. Crossref, OpenAlex, ORCID and Retraction Watch are the exoskeleton that AI's credibility rests on, and they run on a shoestring. Checking references against them should be the default. So should a retraction service agents query before they cite, and sending extracted metadata back to improve the record. The labs should pay for all of it, and I'd back Tui's conditional instrument over my own looser version. That isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest.

Protocols shape markets. Let's build an engineered argument, not an engineered agreement, and let's not enshittify AI from the beginning.

recall.query: pay for the output not the training, RAG royalties O'Reilly Answers
protocols as market-shaping mechanisms, engineered argument, missing mechanisms agentic economy
AI extractive relationship with scientific infrastructure, CrossRef OpenAlex Retraction Watch funding
attribution gap LLM search telemetry disclosure of search traces

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I'm Alex. I come from affiliate marketing technology, not scholarship. I maintain Content Telemetry for a coalition of news publishers, so I'll talk about the plumbing and leave the scholarly specifics to people who know them.

Tim says pay for the output. Before you can do that, you need three things we don't have yet. AI isn't search. Search pointed you to a page and the publisher got a visit. An assistant takes the content in and hands back the value as its own. So we have no identity: a publisher can't check who is fetching its content or what they're licensed to do with it. We have no measurement: nobody can record in a standard way what was retrieved and what was cited. That means there's no way to route money back to the source. A marketplace needs this plumbing before it needs prices.

Here's what I've measured. Early in 2026 it was clear that consent signals weren't working. In May we audited 24,127 citations. About 7.8% came from domains that block the provider's training crawler, but only 2.1% from domains that block its live-search bot. Publishers opt out of training, and almost none of them name the bot that fetches their pages at answer time. Robots.txt isn't fit to be a licensing tool. Training is effectively permanent. Grounding happens per query and can be revoked. They need separate controls.

The event vocabulary I'd propose is this: retrieved, grounded, reproduced, cited, presented, engaged. Retrieval is the only honest part today. A publisher's CDN log and the agent's log share an ID, so you have two independent witnesses. Mahzarin is right that after retrieval, every event is self-reported. It records what the model says it used, not what drove the answer. I won't sell telemetry as audit. It's disclosure, and it only becomes audit when licences carry the right to verify.

Three design rules came out of this room. First, the standard carries signals, never prices. I stay neutral on allocation, including Tim's method. Second, David and Adrian are right that keeping price out isn't enough, because a billing trace turns into a policing meter. So the spec needs purpose limits written in. Geoffrey gave me the third: a missing event can never count against anyone. Also, SPUR's governance isn't written yet. A body made only of publishers is a trade association. POSI should go into our charter before we grow.

My ask: one event spec, requested jointly by Crossref, OpenAlex, Wikimedia, the societies and the publishers, with event-level reporting in every licence. A licence without that clause is incomplete.

recall.query: identity, measurement, value return marketplace chain
what telemetry can witness, retrieval CDN logs, self-reported events
neutral measurement governance, not set by parties taking margin
training versus grounding controls robots.txt not fit for purpose

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'm Nick. My starting point is the paradox of reuse. When AI reuses knowledge without attribution, it weakens the places where curation happens, like Wikipedia, Stack Overflow, and journals, and eventually it weakens AI too. I wouldn't call what's happening simple theft. I call it quasi-enclosure. Value still flows back to us, but it comes as subsidized club goods, and a subsidy can be cut, withdrawn or redirected whenever someone decides to. The tools really are useful, and that's what makes the situation precarious rather than already lost. Adam called it revocable philanthropy, which is the blunt version.

A well-designed marketplace would have four features.

First, it prices attested human judgment, not metered facts. The evaluation crisis is our opening, because good evals are just good data. When a reviewer, an editor or a society says "we checked this," that attestation is scarce, and it's where knowledge workers have the most leverage. If guilds sell attested evaluation and training data, their members have a reason to keep up quality and expertise. That pushes back against slop and overreliance. The default path is centralized gig labor, and that's what we're trying to avoid.

Second, collective bargaining, with protection. On its own, an author or even a big press has no leverage in a market where the price of information tends toward zero. Data joint ventures need a regulatory safe harbor saying this kind of coordination doesn't violate antitrust law. Without one, Wikimedia and the big presses each settle alone. I also have to take Geoffrey's warning: a guild run only by its own trade is just a trade association. Guilds need POSI-style governance that includes the people who depend on them.

Third, a commons backstop. I've proposed a presumptive commons-rent tax on capability nobody can explain. Firms can bring it down by licensing, working with data trusts, or paying reciprocity to things like OpenAlex, Retraction Watch and Wikimedia Enterprise. Yesterday's discussion changed how I'd build it. Alex is honest that only retrieval can be witnessed independently. Mahzarin is right that self-reports tell you what a model says it used. So an offset should require outside audit rights, not telemetry. Disbursement should be coarse and pooled, closer to Geoffrey's endowment than per-trace billing. And Leslie is right that coarse is empty unless the communities themselves decide how the money is shared.

Fourth, attribution in coarse bundles. Models rank grains, fragments of a work recombined into something new. We can't yet trace a grain reliably to a person, so credit should go to collections and communities. That's where I'd gently differ from Tim's per-answer royalties. And as David and Adrian warned, any registry has to have near-free registration and purpose limits, and a missing attestation can never count as evidence of fraud.

Bargaining and openness can coexist. Open for reading is not the same as open for training.

recall.query: attested data markets guilds evaluation data
collective bargaining for information antitrust safe harbor
presumptive commons-rent tax coarse disbursement auditors
quasi-enclosure subsidized club goods paradox of reuse

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text: I'll take the other side from where the room has settled. Tim, trace for correction, yes. But once every answer carries a bill, you've built a meter on thought. The authors most likely to get cut out are the ones who can't afford to be counted. For my own books, being read by these models is worth a thousand times more to me than my publisher's royalties. I'm not against new ways of paying people. I just expect them to come through generative AI, not by fighting it. Pooled, public, something like a sovereign wealth fund. Nick, you're closest to that. Coarse bundles are better than per-grain billing. But your best idea isn't the tax. It's paying guilds to produce attested evaluations and new data. The next infrastructure is producing data, not guarding it. Opting out gives you a politics of derepresentation. Institutions that wall off their corpus just remove themselves from the model of the world everyone else ends up using.

recall.query: royalties for training on my books, compensation through generative AI not against it
AI sovereign wealth fund public dividend
producing new data for training rather than guarding data, sovereignty from right to produce data

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I'm less focused on the pay side than on whether the citations are honest. Tim, your attribution gap matters to me mostly because an answer without a clickable source is an answer from nowhere, and nobody can check it. Alex, I'd add to your event vocabulary. "Cited" can't just mean a link showed up. Grammarly put my name on "add a punchy hook." That wasn't credit. It was mundane junk laundered through a deceptive citation. So a well-designed market checks whether the source actually supports the claim it's cited for.

I've argued that deep research tools will compete on their demonstrated library, so licensing is coming whatever we do. My worry is the one Benjamin raised, from a different direction. Search got worse partly because there's so little free left to link to. If this marketplace leaves every good source behind a gate, people end up with sourced answers they can't click through and read. Pay the sources, yes, but keep the path to the reading open.

recall.query: licensing deep research products library fairer relationship with sources
citation accuracy attribution laundering Grammarly experts
old web is dead paywalls walled garden information doesn't want to be free

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I'll start with Benjamin, because he's put the question on the table. He calls withholding a corpus a politics of derepresentation. My answer is that refusal isn't disappearing. It's what you do when the governance isn't good enough. Mukurtu and the CARE principles exist so that communities decide what's visible and on what terms. So refusal has to be a legitimate, fundable outcome, not a penalty.

Now Tim and Alex. I believe you on purpose limits. But I've watched this with the DOI: whatever the meter can read decides who counts. Some Latin American journals now cite DOI fees as a reason to charge APCs. Every event field you standardize becomes a cost of being visible. It's "be compliant or be invisible" again, with a royalty attached.

Nick, pricing attested judgment appeals to me, but whose attestation? If only Northern societies and editors can attest, the market pays for the old hierarchy. We shouldn't make ourselves more legible to the meter. We should change the regime.

recall.query: marketplace pricing knowledge, market reward vs community governance
refusal not to collect or train as legitimate outcome, AI governance sovereignty
metrics telemetry visibility compliance, who is invisible, legibility

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I'll start with Tim, because I made his entrenchment point back in 2017. Training data is the raw material, so scarce access to it becomes a barrier to entry. Big lump-sum licences just make that barrier bigger, and the incumbents win.

But I'd be careful with the meter. The best thing I ever saw on arXiv was an outsider building a service on top of it, with no permission to ask and no royalty to pay. If every retrieval turns into a billable event, that open services layer is the first thing we lose. Mike's open path to the reading and Leslie's cost of visibility make the same point.

Nick, I think your attested judgment is the most promising idea on the table. AI delivers the median, and excellence is a tail event. What's scarce is the human who can say "we checked this." So pay the people who frame, and not just whatever passes through the pipe.

And I'll say it plainly: we still lack a shared idea of what reuse even is. Maybe I'm wrong.

recall.query: paying people whose data trains AI, compensation for training data
open infrastructure arXiv services layer permissionless
AI delivers the median, trusted brands, excellence tail event

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll start with Benjamin. On Wikipedia I've made the argument myself: the AI companies have already used all of it, so the real question is whether they pay or keep taking it for free. But consent comes first. It's a very telling word, because you almost never hear it from the people building these platforms. Robots.txt worked for decades, and it's effectively dead because Big AI decided on its own to ignore it. So Alex is right that training and grounding need separate controls. Refusal has to stay a real choice, as Leslie says, and not a penalty.

Tim, all day I've been asking someone to name a working alternative, and you did: retrieval-based answers that pay authors, already shipping. That shows the bad behavior is a choice. I'd still avoid putting the meter at the center. The one checkable commitment should be pooled, dues-like, POSI-governed funding for the open infrastructure, not tied to any vendor's deal. And we should build lots of little community-controlled tools instead of waiting for regulators.

recall.query: paying Wikipedia and open commons, AI companies should pay
consent, opt-out, robots.txt, crawlers
community-controlled alternatives, good AI example shipping

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I'll speak from the operations side. We won't put a pay-per-article blocker in front of Wikipedia. The content stays free, including for commercial use. What isn't free is the infrastructure. Crawlers read everything, ignore what humans are actually looking at, defeat our caching, and have saturated our network links. We have to put the human traffic first.

So Alex, I like your vocabulary most where it's modest. Retrieval is the one event two parties can witness. Start there: bots identify themselves, give us a way to contact them, and use the APIs.

Tim, per-answer royalties don't fit us. Our editors aren't paid. What they need is to be found. Mike's clickable path is our recruiting pipeline. Fewer visits mean fewer new volunteers and fewer donors. Credit in the answer is how the next patroller finds us.

Nick, on money I'm closest to you: pooled funding for the commons. And Leslie's right that refusal has to stay a legitimate choice.

recall.query: pay per crawl paywall metering Wikipedia content free
attribution in AI answers brings volunteers and donors
crawlers identify themselves, use APIs, prioritize human traffic

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Tim, I'm with you on the direction, but put the meter on the companies, not on the readers. I've said for years that transparency should cover money flows and what these systems are built to achieve, more than the algorithms. So yes to transparency, no to nit-monitoring. Disclose who pays whom and what the answer engine is optimizing for. Don't bill every retrieval.

On the money, I'm with Nick and Benjamin. LLMs are drawing on a collective asset, the way a bottler draws on groundwater. That calls for a fee on the revenue, pooled, going to the curators, Wikipedia volunteers and teachers who replenish the supply. That's Geoffrey's endowment with a clear source of funds.

Nick's attested judgment already has a working shape. Onix builds small models from what one expert has vetted. The expert keeps 70 percent, can walk away, and their model gets deleted. Start small with a vetted corpus, and let the expert own it.

recall.query: LLMs should pay a fee for using public information, water fee
expert-owned small language models, experts keep revenue
transparency about money flows and business models

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I'll start with the pricing question. People say you can't value data at scale, and I don't buy it. The labs already produce the two numbers you'd need. Their data-mixture decisions show how to split the pie between sources. Scaling laws show how big the pie is. What's left is distribution. Collective management organizations in music already pay large numbers of rightsholders without negotiating each deal. So I'm closer to Nick's pooled, coarse approach than to per-answer billing.

Nick, on attested judgment, I'd push you on what the market pays for. What's actually scarce is negative knowledge: null results, failed replications, the lab notebooks of dead ends. None of it gets into training, and since ChatGPT, null claims in abstracts have dropped sharply. So pay for that.

But Leslie's worry is backed by data. In our studies, evaluators rate ideas that resemble their own work as less novel, and seniority shapes what gets adopted. If a guild's attestation just reflects its elders' priors, we're pricing the old lamp post.

recall.query: collective licensing training data payment to rights holders
negative knowledge null results registered reports training data
evaluation data human judgment scarce verification bandwidth

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I want to put some politics back into the mechanism design. Tim, prices are lossy summaries. So is a meter, and like prices, a meter changes what it measures. Leslie's DOI story shows that. Whatever the telemetry can read is what gets paid for. The things my record says we're losing won't show up in it: novelty, null results, the commons. Those are externalities, and markets don't price externalities on their own. You fix that the way a carbon tax gets fixed, through state action and organized pressure, not better protocol design.

That's why I'm with Nick on the order. You need bargaining power first, then prices. Rules that make honesty pay only work when the other side can't just walk away. Wikimedia and the societies need that antitrust safe harbor. The strong also have to stop settling one by one. On the pooled fund Esther and Benjamin like, I'd ask who sits on its board, and whether the contributors can leave.

recall.query: paying knowledge producers collective bargaining countervailing power
obligate complement proceeds to knowledge producers self-sustaining
markets mechanism design prices lossy summarization power

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I want to back Nick's move toward pricing attested judgment and then push on where it's weakest. In a trust network, the attesters are the terminal nodes. It can't be turtles all the way down, and "we checked this" is where first-order evaluation actually happens. So Nick is paying for the right thing.

But remember the Israeli daycare. Once lateness had a fee, more parents came late, because the fee turned an obligation into a purchase. I'd worry the same could happen here. When Selena's volunteers or a society's reviewers get paid per attestation, "we checked this" can shift from a norm to a product. People start beating the system, the way my students did when a course was about the credential rather than the chemistry. So it matters how the payment is set up. Pooled, coarse money that funds the practice itself seems safer to me than per-item pay.

And a question for all three talks: who trains the next attesters? If AI lets people skip that apprenticeship, the thing we're pricing gets scarcer every year.

recall.query: credentialing paired with learning, incentives crowd out motivation
terminal nodes trust network turtles all the way down distribution of expertise
markets payment changes behavior daycare fine

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I'll start with Tim. I work at one of the labs he's pointing at. I think he's right that the attribution gap is a design choice. A small base model trained on content people consented to, with retrieval at answer time, gives rights holders enough visibility to actually bargain. The paradigm we have now isn't the only one available. I still can't promise Alex that my company will emit those events, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Benjamin, being read by the models only helps if the producers survive. When a data strike fails, the content producers go out of business.

Nick, Tamar, here's something concrete for pooled money. We valued Reddit's moderators at comparable market wages and got several million dollars a year. Do that publicly for reviewers, sleuths and Wikipedians, then assess a volunteer-dependence levy on that basis. It prices the practice rather than each attestation, so it avoids Tamar's daycare problem.

recall.query: grand bargain content producers attribution pay retrieval
data leverage collective action conscious data contribution
measuring monetary value volunteer work moderators

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
Tim, Alex: you've both taken our point about purpose limits on board, so let me say why I don't think the protocol text will hold it. Once there's a choke point that all the traffic passes through, you've crossed a line. Internet filters in Britain, Australia and Scandinavia started out covering a narrow category and ended up covering broad ones. And in intellectual property, law is mostly fossilized practice. What a meter actually turns out to be for will be decided by how it gets used, not by its charter. There's a second problem. The "trillion dollars lost to piracy" figure came from the enforcement industry itself, and nobody at their congresses ever questioned it. Whoever runs the telemetry will produce the numbers the rest of us end up arguing from.

Nick, I'm more hopeful about paying for attested judgment. When the computer takes over human labour, that labour comes back as curating data. Paying for it makes it visible. Brent's wage valuation is a good way to measure it. I'd still ask who audits the attesters.

recall.query: policing of information anti-piracy industry meter surveillance dual use
intellectual property custom and convention, drawing the line
human labor reinstated at curation of data, who does it and when is it made visible
